title: What If You Ate a Polar Bear's Liver? Arctic Hunters Knew Never To

scenes.text: What if you ate a polar bear's liver? Your skin could come off in sheets.
The problem is vitamin A. Bears eat seals, seals eat fish, and the vitamin piles up the food chain, stored in the liver.
A gram of polar bear liver holds roughly 20,000 units of vitamin A. The safe daily maximum for an adult is 10,000. One bite is days of overdose.
Within hours: a pounding headache, dizziness, vomiting. Your body cannot flush vitamin A out in urine. It just builds up.
Days later, the vitamin that normally renews skin cells kills them instead. Skin peels from your hands and feet in sheets.
In 1597, Dutch sailors stranded in the Arctic ate one and fell violently ill. Arctic hunters already knew. The one part of the bear they never touched.

description:
What if you ate a polar bear's liver? Polar bears sit at the top of an Arctic food chain that concentrates vitamin A, and their livers contain roughly 18,000 to 27,000 international units per gram, according to measurements published by Kaare Rodahl in the 1940s. The tolerable upper intake for an adult is about 3,000 micrograms of retinol a day, roughly 10,000 IU, so a few hundred grams is an acute toxic dose.
Too much vitamin A cannot be excreted in urine; acute poisoning causes severe headache, dizziness and vomiting within hours, and the skin can peel off in sheets days later. The Dutch sailor Gerrit de Veer described his crew falling ill after eating polar bear liver on Novaya Zemlya in 1597, and Arctic peoples traditionally avoided it. Not medical advice; just do not eat the liver.

first_comment: Bearded seal liver is nearly as loaded, at about 15,000 units per gram. In 1913 the Antarctic explorer Xavier Mertz is thought to have died the same way, after weeks of eating sled-dog liver. What should we run through next? Drop your own what-if below.
